title: Squandering Attraction: How the Second Trump Administration is Undermining American Soft Power
gist: Sarah Yerkes argues the second Trump administration is deliberately as well as accidentally destroying the sources of U.S. soft power: it has dismantled USAID, hobbled the National Endowment for Democracy, interfered openly in foreign elections and made unpredictability a tactic. Global favorability fell to 35% in 2025, and confidence in Trump (21%) now trails confidence in Xi (31%). Because soft power erodes faster than it can be rebuilt, she expects Washington to rely more on costlier coercion while China and Russia fill the vacuum.

themes.theme: Soft power as force multiplier for hard power

insights.claim: Soft power alone cannot meet U.S. national security needs, but hard power has limits too, as the current U.S. war against Iran shows; soft power makes hard power more efficient by encouraging cooperation and compliance that reduce the need for force.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Loss of attraction raises the cost of achieving U.S. aims, which implies more spending on sanctions, inducements and military action.
insights.quote: Soft power allows for more effective and efficient use of hard power than hard power alone, as it encourages cooperation and compliance which deters the need for hard power.
insights.locator: Soft power on its own is insufficient

insights.claim: Joseph Nye's concept of 'smart power' holds that the most effective use of power combines hard and soft power, each amplifying the other, and both states and non-state actors such as terrorist groups rely on soft power for recruitment and legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: A useful lens for judging whether coercive U.S. policy such as tariffs and sanctions will get compliance or set off hedging.
insights.locator: What Is Soft Power?

insights.claim: Yerkes compares soft power to corporate reputation: its effect in any single case is hard to isolate, much like the effect of a brand on consumer demand, but it is hard to believe it has no effect.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Treat soft-power erosion as slow-moving brand damage to the U.S. that is hard to measure in real time.
insights.locator: He expanded the definition after 9/11

themes.theme: Favorability data and the historical cycle

insights.claim: Pew's average favorability of the United States across surveyed countries went from 63% in 2002 to 33% in 2004, recovered to 55% in 2009 and peaked at 63% in 2015. It fell to 36% in 2020, rebounded to 61% in 2021 and dropped again to 35% in 2025.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Global favorability swings sharply with each administration, and the 2025 reading is near the all-time lows set after the Iraq invasion.
insights.locator: The ups and downs of American soft power

insights.claim: After the 2003 Iraq invasion, U.S. favorability fell from 75% to 48% in Britain, 70% to 34% in Italy, 61% to 25% in Germany, 63% to 31% in France and 61% to 28% in Russia, according to Pew.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Shows how fast a single policy shock can collapse allied public opinion; the past precedent for today's decline.
insights.locator: Over the past twenty-five years

insights.claim: Guantanamo and Abu Ghraib, the response to Hurricane Katrina, the 2010 WikiLeaks cables, Snowden's 2013 NSA revelations and the U.S. failure to ratify treaties such as the Rome Statute and Kyoto all chipped away at U.S. soft power before Trump.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Erosion of U.S. soft power is cumulative and bipartisan, so recovery starts from an already-diminished base.
insights.locator: The controversies around the treatment of prisoners

insights.claim: U.S. soft power has historically declined and mostly recovered: Nye noted the 1960s, with assassinations, Vietnam and domestic bombings, were worse than Trump's first term, and those shocks pushed leaders to work to restore U.S. attractiveness. Yerkes warns that past recovery does not guarantee recovery this time.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: The base case of a rebound after the administration ends is not assured; investors should not assume mean reversion in allied trust.
insights.quote: However, the fact that American soft power recovered from harm in the past does not mean it will do so this time.
insights.locator: American soft power has declined before

themes.theme: First Trump term vs Biden repair

insights.claim: The first Trump administration openly chose a 'hard-power budget' and withdrew from the Paris Agreement, the TPP and the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA). Under that administration the U.S. fell from 1st to 6th in the 2021 Global Soft Power Index, and the EIU downgraded it to a 'flawed democracy'.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Rankings and indices give measurable proxies for tracking U.S. reputational risk.
insights.quote: It is not a soft-power budget. This is a hard-power budget, and that was done intentionally.
insights.locator: The First Trump Administration

insights.claim: Cultural and educational soft power, including Olympic dominance, exports of creative services and flows of international students and tourists, held up during Trump's first term even as political credibility fell.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Cultural soft power has been resilient before, so the immigration and visa curbs of the second term are the new risk to watch for education and tourism flows.
insights.locator: Some components of U.S. soft power

insights.claim: The limits of coercion in Trump's first term showed when Europe built a special payment mechanism to get around the U.S. JCPOA withdrawal, few nations joined the campaign against the WHO, and support was weak for removing Venezuela's Maduro.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Allies building workarounds to U.S. sanctions is a precedent for wider efforts to reduce dependence on dollar payment rails.
insights.locator: The first Trump administration demonstrated the limits

insights.claim: The Biden administration rebuilt soft power by rejoining Paris and the WHO, delivering over 693 million vaccine doses to developing countries, launching the G7 Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment against China's Belt and Road, and hosting Summits for Democracy. The chaotic Afghanistan withdrawal and support for Israel in Gaza undercut those gains.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
entities: Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment
insights.so_what: A policy reversal after an administration change can restore favorability quickly, as the jump to 61% in 2021 showed.
insights.locator: The Biden Administration

themes.theme: Second Trump term: dismantling soft-power institutions

insights.claim: The second Trump administration is unique because it is destroying traditional sources and instruments of U.S. soft power, both intentionally and unintentionally, doing damage that may not be repaired for decades.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Points to a structural, multi-decade decline in U.S. influence rather than a cyclical dip.
insights.quote: it is unintentionally and intentionally destroying traditional sources and instruments of American soft power, doing damage that may not be repaired for decades
insights.locator: Most indicators demonstrate that American soft power

insights.claim: The administration has dismantled USAID, hobbled the National Endowment for Democracy, frozen hiring in foreign-assistance bodies and sought to close Voice of America and the U.S. Institute of Peace. Research shows U.S. foreign aid, especially health aid, measurably boosts favorable views of the U.S.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Cutting aid removes a proven, low-cost lever of influence and creates openings for Chinese development finance in the Global South.
insights.locator: The clearest example is the destruction of USAID

insights.claim: The 2025 National Security Strategy does not reject soft power; it reframes it around 'inherent greatness' and respect for other governing systems. That reframing courts autocrats rather than projecting democracy, equality and human rights.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: U.S. policy now favors deals with illiberal governments, which shifts which partner countries benefit from U.S. support.
insights.locator: The Second Trump Administration

insights.claim: The Trump administration has openly tried to sway elections in at least twelve countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Germany, Hungary, Canada, Japan and the UK, by endorsing mainly illiberal or far-right candidates or by tying aid to electoral outcomes. This breaks with the post-1980s U.S. norm of nonpartisan democracy assistance.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: U.S. political intervention adds election-related risk in allied markets and damages trust with democratic allies.
insights.locator: The Trump administration has also overtly attempted

insights.claim: Restricting immigration, including shutting out or deporting scientists, doctors and other experts, along with violent enforcement crackdowns, damages the 'city on a hill' attraction on which U.S. soft power rests.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Reduced inflows of foreign talent are a long-run headwind for U.S. research, universities and the tech labor supply.
insights.locator: The Trump administration’s actions on immigration

insights.claim: Punitive, indiscriminate tariffs, threats to annex Greenland and talk of retaking the Panama Canal have damaged U.S. trustworthiness. Citing Keren Yarhi-Milo, Yerkes says Trump has undermined U.S. credibility more than any past president, and has done so deliberately by seeking to be unpredictable.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: A higher risk premium on commitments to U.S. allies; expect allies to hedge in trade, defense and reserve choices.
insights.locator: Insofar as soft power flows from the credibility

insights.claim: Contrary to Trump's view, deliberate unreliability is not a strength: allies will not comply when rewards are not guaranteed, and personalist alliances may push allies to raise military spending and hedge against the United States.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Supports a structural rise in allied defense budgets and in strategic-autonomy policies, especially in Europe.
insights.quote: Contrary to his argument, Trump’s intentional unreliability is not a strength—it harms American soft power as allies question U.S. reliability and adversaries see this as weakness.
insights.locator: Contrary to his argument

insights.claim: Trump treats soft power as his personal brand (MAGA hats as gifts to leaders, diplomacy held at Mar-a-Lago and his golf clubs), and Yerkes says he repurposes it for his own and his family's financial benefit.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Access to deals runs through personal channels, so relationships with leaders matter more than institutions and policy may not outlast this president.
insights.quote: For Trump, soft power is also more about his personal brand than that of the United States.
insights.locator: For Trump, soft power is also more about

insights.claim: Pew data show median confidence across 20 countries fell from 54% for Biden in 2023 to 21% for Trump in 2026, while confidence in Xi rose from 19% to 31%, so China's leader is now more trusted than the U.S. president.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: A measurable flip in leader trust in China's favor, which helps Beijing compete for partners on trade and technology.
insights.locator: One possible consequence for American soft power

insights.claim: Because Trump's approach to soft power is so tied to him personally, a future administration of either party could hardly continue it.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Implies a likely policy break after Trump, a scenario to factor into long-dated geopolitical positioning.

themes.theme: China benefits and the costly turn to coercion

insights.claim: Analysts cited by Yerkes argue that America First policy is driving people closer to China and giving others license to build stronger links to Beijing, which raises China's relative attractiveness as a partner.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Supports a view of growing Chinese diplomatic and commercial reach in hedging countries.
insights.locator: Some analysts have argued, based on polling

insights.claim: The decline in U.S. soft power leaves a vacuum for China and Russia, which use U.S. dysfunction such as January 6 to argue that 'democracy produces chaos' and that autocracy brings stability.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Strengthens the authoritarian bloc's narrative pull in contested regions.
insights.locator: There are several important long-term implications

insights.claim: Soft power is easier to destroy than rebuild, yet its sources are diffuse and change slowly. The full damage may not show until well after the administration ends: January 6 produced no measurable drop in Hollywood box office receipts or foreign student enrollment.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Watch lagging indicators such as foreign student enrollment, tourism, box office and aid demand for delayed signs of decline.
insights.quote: The dimensions of soft power that the Trump administration has damaged are easier to erode than to rebuild.
insights.locator: What Comes Next?

insights.claim: As U.S. attractiveness falls, Washington will probably have to pursue its goals through costlier means such as financial inducements, sanctions or force, which also risk more hostile blowback.
insights.speaker: Sarah Yerkes
insights.so_what: Points to heavier use of sanctions and tariffs and higher defense spending, with geopolitical risk premia to match.
insights.quote: This is an expensive and potentially dangerous path forward for the United States.
insights.locator: As its attractiveness and legitimacy erode
